newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE-Pakistan MQM to fight polls despite harrassment.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Pakistan MQM to fight polls despite harrassment.

text.p: Hundreds of young men throng narrow lanes near the headquarters of Karachi's ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM) to hear a speech relayed by telephone and loudspeaker from their London-based leader.
The party activists crowded round the modest home of Altaf Hussain, in self-exile since 1992, would have feared to venture there before the downfall of Benazir Bhutto on November 5.
The MQM articulates the grievances of the Mohajir community, which forms a majority of Karachi's estimated 12 million people.
Many Mohajirs, Urdu-speaking migrants who settled in Pakistan after the partition of the Indian sub-continent in 1947, feel they are victims of discrimination.
Friction with Karachi's other ethnic groups, who include Sindhis, Pashtuns and Balochis, has often spilled into violence and clashes with police, paramilitary rangers and troops.

President Farooq Leghari's dismissal of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) for alleged corruption and misrule eased the immediate pressure on the MQM, whose activists were hunted relentlessly during Bhutto's three years in power.

The MQM is now using its relative freedom to campaign for national and provincial elections set for February 3, but its leaders say party workers still face harrassment from the security forces and violence from a splinter MQM faction.

"Only extra-judicial killings have stopped and public addresses by Altaf Hussain have been allowed, but our activists are still being harrassed and arrested to join thousands of others already in jail," said Shoaib Bukhari, an MQM leader.
So far the campaign is low-key, with local MQM units holding religious meetings to honour militants killed in recent years.
"We will take part in the elections and are sure to get at least 16 National Assembly and 32 provincial assembly seats," Bukhari tol Reuters in Karachi, the MQM's power-base.

"Although Farooq Leghari used extra-judicial killings of our activists as one of the charges for dismissing the Bhutto regime, nobody has been brought to book for the killings, nor has the behaviour of the Karachi police or the new caretaker provincial government changed towards the MQM," Bukhari said.
He said MQM candidates in districts "under the occupation of terrorists" of the breakaway MQM-Haqiqi had been unable to open their election offices or hold campaign rallies.
"Our candidates and activists in these areas are under threat of their lives," he said, accusing police and Haqiqi supporters of attacking several newly opened election offices.
"Unless the police ensure security of the candidates...how are we supposed to run the campaign?" Bukhari asked.
The MQM-Haqiqi won no seats at the last election in 1993.
The mainstream MQM boycotted the 1993 National Assembly (lower house) polls in protest of an army sweep in Karachi that had put many of its leaders in jail or forced them into hiding.
In a sudden switch, the MQM opted to fight provincial polls the next day, winning 28 of the 100 Sindh assembly seats.
Many people have died since June 19, 1992 when the army launched a crackdown on the MQM in the towns and cities of Sindh, alleging that it was involved in criminal activities.
The army withdrew in late 1994, but in June 1995 Bhutto ordered a new security drive, accusing MQM militants of killing hundreds of security men and political foes in targeted attacks.
The struggle accounted for most of the 2,000 or more deaths in ethnic, political and sectarian strife in Karachi in 1995. Police put the death toll at 800 in 1994 and 500 in 1996.
For now, the violence has receded. Bukhari said Hussain had told his loyalists to show restraint even if the attitude of the security forces left them still feeling insecure.
"Despite these difficulties, February 3 will show that the MQM has increased its popularity, not only in urban Sindh but throughout Pakistan," Bukhari declared.
The MQM has fielded 58 candidates in Sindh for national and provincial assembly seats, and 28 for seats in other provinces.
Bukhari said the MQM had made no electoral pacts or pledges to back anyone for prime minister, but would support any party prepared to help implement the MQM's 18-point manifesto.
